title: Product & work breakdown structures (PBS, WBS)
blurb: Use a PBS to show what will be delivered and a WBS to show the work, and explain how together they define the scope.
question: A sports club is refurbishing its pavilion. The sponsor wants to see, on one page, exactly what the club will get, and the project manager needs a list of every piece of work to estimate and schedule. Which two structures should the project manager produce, in what order, and how do they relate?

teach.body: A whole project is too big to estimate, plan or hand to anyone. So the scope is broken down, level by level, into smaller and smaller parts until each one is manageable. Two hierarchies do this job. The product breakdown structure (PBS) answers WHAT will be delivered. The work breakdown structure (WBS) answers what WORK must be done to deliver it. Together they illustrate the full scope of the project.

A PBS is a hierarchical breakdown of the products (deliverables) the project will produce. The top box is the final product; each level splits it into its component products, sub-assemblies and parts. Items are written as nouns: things you could point at or hand over. Its main use is to get the sponsor, users and team to agree exactly what will be delivered before anyone plans the work.

teach.caption: Every box is a product, a noun. Nothing here says how, when or who.

teach.body: A WBS is a hierarchical breakdown of the work needed to deliver the products. It is usually derived from the PBS: for each product, ask 'what work produces this?'. Items are written as verbs or activities. The lowest level is the work package: a piece of work small enough to be estimated, scheduled, costed, assigned to an owner and controlled. Project management work itself belongs in the WBS too.

teach.h: WBS derived from the pavilion PBS
teach.caption: Each product from the PBS now has the work that creates it. Numbering lets every work package be referenced in estimates, the schedule and the budget.

teach.body: Together the PBS and WBS define the full scope: every product and every piece of work that is in scope appears, and nothing that is not. That makes them powerful control tools. A product with no work under it shows a gap in the plan; work that produces no agreed product is a warning sign of scope creep or gold plating. At Hollins Park, if 'new floodlights' appears in neither structure, it is simply not in scope.

steps.label: Cost and assign
steps.sub: Budget each package, name an owner

teach.caption: The WBS is the basis for estimating, scheduling, costing and assigning work.

teach.text: PBS = products (nouns, WHAT is delivered). WBS = work (verbs, the WORK to deliver it). Watch for distractors claiming the WBS shows the order or timing of work (that is the schedule), the people involved (that is the OBS), or the costs (that is the CBS).

items: PBS: a hierarchy of the products or deliverables: WHAT the project will deliver.
WBS: a hierarchy of the work needed to deliver those products, usually derived from the PBS.
The lowest level of a WBS is the work package: estimable, assignable and controllable.
Together they illustrate the full scope: everything in scope, nothing extra.
The WBS is the basis for estimating, scheduling, costing and assigning work.

summary: You can now describe a PBS as the hierarchy of what the project will deliver and a WBS as the hierarchy of the work to deliver it. You can also explain how one is derived from the other and why, together, they define the full scope and underpin estimating, scheduling, costing and assigning work.

A.q: What does a product breakdown structure (PBS) show?
options: The work to make each product
The cost of each part of the work
A.why: A PBS is a hierarchical breakdown of the products or deliverables: what the project will deliver.

whyNot.0: The work needed to make each product is shown in the work breakdown structure.
whyNot.1: Teams and people are shown in the organisational breakdown structure.
whyNot.3: Costs are broken down in the cost breakdown structure.

A.q: Which of the following items would you expect to find in a WBS rather than a PBS?
A.why: 'Install panels' is an activity (a verb), so it is work and belongs in the WBS. The others are products.

whyNot.0: A solar panel array is a product, so it belongs in the PBS.
whyNot.2: Changing rooms are a product the project delivers, so they belong in the PBS.
whyNot.3: A training guide is a document the project hands over, so it is a product in the PBS.

A.q: What is the lowest level of a work breakdown structure usually called?
A.why: The lowest level of a WBS is the work package: a unit of work that can be estimated, scheduled, assigned and controlled.

whyNot.0: A milestone is a significant point or event in the schedule, with no duration of its own.
whyNot.1: A cost account belongs to the cost breakdown structure.
whyNot.3: Configuration items are products and documents under configuration management, not WBS levels.

B.q: Why is a PBS usually produced before the WBS?
options: The PBS sets the order of the work
The work is derived from the products
A sponsor cannot approve a WBS
The WBS needs the budget agreed first
B.why: Once the products are agreed, the work to create each one can be worked out, so the WBS is derived from the PBS.

whyNot.0: Neither structure shows the order of work; sequencing happens in the schedule.
whyNot.2: There is no rule preventing a sponsor approving a WBS.
whyNot.3: The budget is built up from the WBS, so it cannot be needed first.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following does a work breakdown structure directly support?
1. Estimating
2. Scheduling
3. Assigning work
4. Setting the organisation's strategy
B.why: The WBS is the basis for estimating, scheduling, costing and assigning the work.

whyNot.0: Organisational strategy is set at portfolio and senior level, not from a project's WBS.
whyNot.1: Organisational strategy is not set from a WBS, and estimating is missing from this option.
whyNot.2: Organisational strategy is not set from a WBS, and scheduling is missing from this option.

B.q: Complete the statement: used together, the PBS and WBS should capture...
options: all of the scope, and nothing extra
the order the work will be done in
who approved each change to scope
the budget for each life cycle phase
B.why: Together the PBS and WBS define the full scope: everything in scope appears, and nothing outside it.

whyNot.1: Ordering the work is the job of the schedule, not the breakdown structures.
whyNot.2: Change approvals are recorded through change control and configuration records.
whyNot.3: Budgets are set out in the cost breakdown structure and budget, built from the WBS.

C.q: On a website project, the PBS includes an 'Accessibility statement page', but the WBS contains no work to produce it. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The WBS is missing some work
The page is out of scope
C.why: Every product in the PBS should have work in the WBS that produces it. A product with no work under it means the WBS is incomplete.

whyNot.0: The page is an agreed product, so it is not 'extra'; the gap is in the work.
whyNot.2: Being in the agreed PBS means the page is in scope.
whyNot.3: The OBS shows people and teams; the gap here is missing work, not missing people.

C.q: Which statement about a work breakdown structure is correct?
options: It shows the critical path of the work
It lists people and reporting lines
It is only drawn up after the work has started
It is not a schedule: it has no time order
C.why: A WBS is a hierarchy of the work, not a sequence. The order and timing of work are worked out later, in the schedule.

whyNot.0: The critical path comes from network analysis of the schedule, not the WBS.
whyNot.1: People and reporting lines are shown in the organisational breakdown structure.
whyNot.2: The WBS is produced during planning so it can drive estimates and the schedule.

C.q: A project manager wants an analytical (bottom-up) estimate of the project. Which structure must be in place first?
C.why: Analytical estimating builds the estimate up from each work package, so a detailed WBS is needed first.

whyNot.1: The OBS shows who is involved, but bottom-up estimates are built from the work packages.
whyNot.2: A risk register informs contingency, but it is not the basis of a bottom-up estimate.
whyNot.3: A power/interest grid is for stakeholder analysis, not estimating.

reteach.title: Planning a music festival
reteach.question: You're organising a one-day village music festival. How would you list what the festival will have, and then the jobs needed to make each thing happen?

blocks.h: First the things, then the jobs
blocks.body: Start with what festival-goers will actually get: a stage, food stalls, toilets, tickets. That list of things is your PBS. Then, for each thing, list the jobs: hire the stage, book the bands, sign up caterers, print and sell tickets. That list of jobs is your WBS. If 'fireworks' is in neither list, nobody is buying fireworks.

blocks.caption: Ask 'what work produces this?' for every product, and the WBS builds itself.

blocks.text: Nouns for the PBS (stage, stalls, tickets). Verbs for the WBS (hire, book, sell).

explain.body: A whole project cannot be estimated, planned or delegated in one go. Breaking it into a hierarchy turns it into small, manageable pieces, makes it easier to spot gaps, and gives everyone a shared picture of the scope.

test.q: What is the main reason for breaking a project's scope down into a hierarchy?
options: To fix the order of the work
test.why: Breaking scope down produces pieces small enough to understand, estimate, plan, assign and control.

whyNot.1: Breakdown structures do not set the order of work; the schedule does.
whyNot.2: Breakdown structures support scope control, but change control is still needed.
whyNot.3: Strategy is set by the organisation; breakdown structures describe a project's scope.

explain.body: A hierarchy of the products or deliverables the project will produce: WHAT will be delivered. Items are nouns. It builds a shared understanding of the end product, so the sponsor and team agree the deliverables before the work is planned.

test.q: Items in a product breakdown structure are usually written as:
options: the dates of the key milestones
test.why: A PBS lists products, so its items are nouns: things that will be delivered.

whyNot.0: Verbs describing tasks belong in the WBS.
whyNot.1: Team members appear in the OBS and RAM, not the PBS.
whyNot.2: Milestone dates belong in the schedule.

explain.body: A hierarchy of the work needed to deliver the products, usually derived from the PBS. Items are verbs or activities. Its lowest level is the work package, which can be estimated, scheduled, costed, assigned and controlled.

test.q: A work breakdown structure is usually derived from which structure?
test.why: The WBS is usually derived from the PBS: for each product, the work needed to create it is identified.

whyNot.0: The OBS shows the people and teams; it is combined with the WBS to make a RAM.
whyNot.1: The CBS is aligned to the WBS, so it comes after it, not before.
whyNot.3: The RAM is built from the WBS and OBS, so it comes after the WBS.

explain.body: If something is in the PBS and WBS, it is in scope; if not, it is out. Checking that every product has work beneath it, and every piece of work produces an agreed product, keeps the plan complete and guards against scope creep.

test.q: During planning, a team member adds a WBS task that produces no product in the agreed PBS. What should the project manager suspect?
options: The PBS is now out of date
The task is a work package
The OBS is missing a whole team
test.why: Work that produces no agreed product is outside the agreed scope, a warning sign of scope creep or gold plating.

whyNot.0: The PBS is the agreed baseline of products; it should not change just because someone added a task.
whyNot.2: Being at the lowest level does not make work legitimate; it must deliver an agreed product.
whyNot.3: The issue is unplanned work, not a missing team.
